after: ## Theories of rights: where do rights come from?
alt: Three theories of where rights come from. Natural rights exist because people are human (Locke, Paine, the UDHR’s inherent dignity): a standard to criticise unjust law, but with no agreed list. Positivism says rights come from law (Bentham; Hart’s minimum content of natural law): enforceable, but removable by the state. Dworkin’s rights as trumps override collective goals and protect minorities, but give judges a large role.
caption: Natural rights, positivism and trumps each answer the source question differently.

after: ## Theories of rights: where do rights come from?
alt: Will theory (Hart): a right gives control to enforce or waive another’s duty, but struggles with young children, people lacking capacity and unwaivable rights. Interest theory (Raz): well-being is sufficient reason to impose a duty, but risks treating every interest as a right. The Convention fits the interest theory: Article 2 protects those who cannot choose, and freedom from torture cannot be waived.
caption: The Convention protects people who cannot choose, so interest theory fits it better.

alt: Hohfeld’s four positions and their correlatives: claim-right and duty (a right to be paid, a duty to pay); liberty and no-right (free to walk on public land, no right to stop it); power and liability (making a will); immunity and disability (the state lacks power to remove a protected status). A claim-right imposes a duty on another; a liberty does not.
caption: A right puts a duty on someone else; a liberty does not.

alt: Before 1998 the UK relied on residual liberties: anything not forbidden was allowed, which Dicey thought the ordinary courts protected well. But the state could also do anything not forbidden: in Malone, telephone tapping was lawful and Mr Malone had no right of privacy. A right places a duty on the state to justify interference. Berlin contrasted negative liberty (freedom from interference) with positive liberty (capacity to act).
caption: A liberty gave Malone nothing to assert; a right makes the state justify itself.

alt: Vasak’s three generations: civil and political rights (life, liberty, expression), where the ECHR mainly sits; economic, social and cultural rights (work, health, education); and collective rights (development, environment). Universality (Vienna Declaration 1993) is set against cultural relativism. Below: the hierarchy of rights, conflicts between rights, responsibilities in Article 10.2, and who holds rights (Sunday Times v UK).
caption: The ECHR covers mainly first-generation rights, held mainly against the state.

after: ## Annotated plan: "Discuss the view that human rights are no more than liberties granted by law."
alt: Seven steps in the essay plan: define right and liberty using Hohfeld; positivist support from Bentham and the HRA; natural rights against (Locke, UDHR); the failure of residual liberties in Malone; Dworkin’s trumps; absolute rights such as Article 3; and a conclusion that legal recognition enforces rights but their justification is moral.
caption: Define, argue both ways with theorists and cases, then judge.
